questions.question: A spinner is divided into 8 equal parts. 5 parts are red, 2 parts are blue, and 1 part is green. You spin the pointer one time. Which colour is the spinner most likely to land on, and why?
options: Red, because 5 of the 8 equal parts are red — more than any other colour
Green, because there is only 1 green part, so green is the special one
Blue, because 2 blue parts is right in the middle between 1 and 5
Red, blue and green all have the same chance, because there are 3 colours on the spinner
questions.explain: To predict one spin, compare how many equal parts each colour covers: red has 5 of 8, blue 2 of 8, green 1 of 8, so red is most likely. The common trap is thinking 3 colours means each colour gets the same chance — the number of parts is what counts, not the number of colours.

questions.question: A spinner has 10 equal parts. 9 parts are yellow and 1 part is purple. You spin it once. Landing on purple is best described as:
options: Likely, because purple is one of the colours printed on the spinner
Unlikely, because only 1 of the 10 equal parts is purple
Equally likely as yellow, because both colours are on the same spinner
Impossible, because there is just one purple part
questions.explain: Purple covers 1 out of 10 equal parts, so it can happen but hardly ever — that is ‘unlikely’. Two traps to avoid: purple is not impossible (it does have a part), and it is not equally likely as yellow just because both colours appear.

questions.question: A spinner has 6 equal parts, labelled 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12. You spin it one time. How likely is it that the pointer lands on an odd number?
options: Unlikely, because most parts are even but a few spins will still land on odd
Equally likely as landing on an even number, because a number is either odd or even
Impossible, because every one of the 6 parts holds an even number
Certain, because the spinner always stops on a number
questions.explain: Check the make-up of the spinner first: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 are all even, so 0 of the 6 parts is odd and the outcome cannot happen — it is impossible. The trap is thinking odd and even always split the chances evenly; here the spinner simply has no odd parts.

questions.question: A spinner has 12 equal parts: 6 are blue, 3 are red, and 3 are green. Which prediction about one spin is best?
options: Every colour has the same chance, because 3 colours share the spinner
Green is the most likely colour, because 3 green parts is a big group
Blue and red are equally likely, because they are the two biggest groups
Blue is the most likely colour, because 6 of the 12 equal parts are blue — about half the spinner
questions.explain: Compare the parts: blue 6 of 12 (half), red 3 of 12, green 3 of 12, so blue is most likely and red and green tie. The trap is giving each colour the same chance because there are 3 colours — the size of each colour's share decides the prediction.

questions.question: A bag holds 10 linking cubes: 4 green, 4 blue and 2 white. Priya takes one cube without looking. Which statement about this draw is true?
options: Green and blue are equally likely, and white is the least likely
Drawing white is impossible, because only 2 cubes are white
All three colours are equally likely, because the bag holds 3 colours
Green is more likely than blue, because green is listed first
questions.explain: Count each colour out of the 10 cubes: green 4, blue 4, white 2 — equal counts mean an equal chance, and the smallest count is the least likely. The trap is assuming every colour has the same chance just because 3 colours are in the bag.

questions.question: A number cube has 6 faces marked 1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3. Nathan rolls it once. Which number should he predict, and why?
options: 1, 2 and 3 are equally likely, because the cube shows three different numbers
3, because 3 of the 6 faces show a 3
2, because 2 sits in the middle of the numbers on the cube
1, because 1 is the smallest number and appears first on the cube
questions.explain: Count the faces, not the different numbers: 3 appears on 3 faces, 1 on 2 faces, 2 on only 1 face, so 3 is the best prediction. The trap is thinking three different numbers means each has the same chance.

questions.question: For a school raffle, Ms. Chan puts 20 tickets in a box: 12 blue and 8 orange. She pulls out one ticket without looking. What should the class predict?
options: Blue and orange are equally likely, because there are only two colours in the box
Orange is more likely, because 8 tickets is still a lot of tickets
Blue is more likely, because 12 of the 20 tickets are blue
It is certain to be blue, because blue has the larger number of tickets
questions.explain: Compare the two amounts out of the total: 12 blue beats 8 orange out of 20, so blue is more likely — but not certain, since orange tickets are in the box too. The trap is treating two colours as an automatic even split, or turning ‘more likely’ into ‘certain’.

questions.question: A prize spinner has 5 equal parts showing these amounts: $1, $1, $1, $2, $5. One spin decides the prize. Which amount is the best prediction?
options: $5, because it is the biggest prize on the spinner
$2, because it is between $1 and $5
$1, $2 and $5 are equally likely, because each amount is printed on the spinner
$1, because 3 of the 5 equal parts show $1
questions.explain: Predict from how much of the spinner each amount covers: $1 fills 3 of the 5 equal parts, while $2 and $5 fill 1 part each, so $1 is the best prediction. The trap is giving each printed amount the same chance — repeated parts change the chances.

questions.question: A spinner is NOT split evenly: red covers half of the spinner, blue covers one quarter, and yellow covers one quarter. Ravi says, ‘There are 3 colours, so each colour has 1 chance out of 3.’ Is Ravi correct?
options: Ravi is wrong — red covers half the spinner, so red alone is just as likely as blue and yellow put together
Ravi is correct, because the pointer can stop anywhere on the spinner
Ravi is wrong — blue and yellow together fill more than red, so blue alone is the most likely colour
Ravi is correct, because there are 3 colours and only 1 pointer
questions.explain: On an uneven spinner, chances come from the size of each share: red is one half, blue one quarter, yellow one quarter, so red equals blue and yellow combined. The trap is Ravi's: counting colours instead of measuring how much space each colour covers.

questions.question: Lena wants to build a marble bag where drawing a red marble is LIKELY but not CERTAIN. Which bag should she make?
options: A bag with 10 red marbles and nothing else
A bag with 8 red and 2 blue marbles
A bag with 4 red, 4 blue and 4 green marbles, since every colour has the same chance anyway
A bag with 2 red and 8 blue marbles
questions.explain: ‘Likely but not certain’ means red must take up most of the bag while at least one other marble remains, and 8 red out of 10 does exactly that. The traps are an all-red bag (that is certain, not likely) and an even mix of colours, which only makes red equally likely, not likely.

questions.question: A spinner has 10 equal parts: 7 green and 3 orange. During recess, Marcus spins it 4 times and records this tally: orange, orange, orange, orange. What should he predict for the 5th spin?
options: Green and orange are now equally likely, because both colours have appeared in the experiment
Orange, because orange has come up 4 times in a row and is on a streak
Green, because 7 of the 10 equal parts are still green — the spinner does not remember earlier spins
No prediction is possible, because the tally shows the make-up of the spinner cannot be trusted
questions.explain: Every spin starts fresh, so predict from the make-up: 7 green parts out of 10 still makes green more likely, even after four oranges in a row. The trap is letting a short tally take over — a run of results does not change how many parts each colour covers.

questions.question: For a field trip, Mr. Singh has a snack bin with 6 apple bars, 4 berry bars and 2 lemon bars. Before the bus leaves he adds 6 more lemon bars, mixes them up, and lets a student take one bar without looking. Which flavour should the class predict?
options: Apple, because apple started out with the most bars in the bin
Apple, berry and lemon are now equally likely, because 3 flavours are in the bin
Lemon is certain, because 6 lemon bars were just added to the bin
Lemon, because there are now 8 lemon bars, more than the 6 apple or the 4 berry
questions.explain: First update the counts after the change — apple 6, berry 4, lemon 2 + 6 = 8, for 18 bars in all — then compare, so lemon is now the most likely draw. Two traps here: predicting from the old counts before the bars were added, and turning ‘most likely’ into ‘certain’ when apple and berry bars are still in the bin.
